evidence.excerpt:
Deep research agents investigate complex questions through itera-
tive search, source examination, and evidence synthesis. A conven-
tional workflow alternates reasoning with individual search and
reading actions. Search as Code introduces a new paradigm: agents
write programs that compose search, source reading, reranking,
model calls, and local processing, returning selected observations
for further reasoning. To support this workflow in existing coding
agents, we presentOpenSaC, an open-source Python library with a
companion Search as Code skill. Configurable capability interfaces
let agents combine these operations while retaining evidence for
inspection and reuse. Compared with standard Codex using its
built-in web search, theOpenSaCconfiguration uses less execution
time and fewer model tokens on BrowseComp and WideSearch,
with higher accuracy on BrowseComp and slightly lower row

evidence.excerpt:
OpenSaCseparates the agent's research decisions from program
execution. The coding agent chooses the next steps and writes a
Python program that combines software development kit (SDK)
calls with local computation and file operations. The library supplies
typed interfaces for search, content fetching, reranking, and model
calls; the host executes the program. Selected execution results
return to the agent, which decides whether to answer or investigate
further. These observations can include source excerpts, extracted
records, computed summaries, or errors.
Figure 2 illustrates a possible labor-statistics program. Indepen-
dent searches cover unemployment, employment, and earnings
series; the program merges rankings, selects URLs, fetches data,
and retains responses before returning records. Grouping known
requests leaves the agent to identify gaps and decide on follow-up
queries.

The host executes programs and provides a workspace for retained
evidence. The synchronous SDK bridges to an asynchronous run-
time that manages capability calls.
Supporting Search as Code.Programs use the host's workspace
to retain sources and intermediate results across executions. They
can save full documents with their URLs, return selected excerpts,
and reuse saved text in later programs. Local helpers complement
this workspace: fuse merges ranked lists through weighted re-
ciprocal rank fusion, and dedup removes repeated identities. Both
preserve original objects, default to exact URL keys, and accept
custom keys. Together, local helpers and ordinary file operations
let programs combine evidence, retain sources, and select what to
return to the agent.
Supporting reliable execution.The runtime bounds concur-
rent provider requests, applies per-request timeouts, and validates
inputs

evidence.excerpt:
Research workflows may require different search services, content
readers, or model endpoints. Provider dispatch separates these back-
end choices from program composition, allowing each capability
to be configured independently.
Adapters map shared capability contracts to each backend's
request and response formats. They register through Python entry
points; the runtime routes calls to the configured adapter for each
capability. Included adapters support Serper and Jina Reader, HTTP
backends, and model endpoints compatible with the OpenAI API.
Users can combine services, replace backends while retaining
program logic, or compare provider configurations with the same
program. Developers can connect new services through custom
adapters without modifying the core library (Figure 2).

evidence.excerpt:
OpenSaCpairs the library with a companion Search as Code skill
that guides agents in composing research programs. The library
supplies executable capabilities; the skill explains when to batch in-
dependent requests, preserve sources, select observations, and reuse
evidence. This guidance is provided through the skill mechanisms
of coding agents such as Codex and Claude Code [2, 6].
The skill works with the agent's existing Python execution and
file tools. Users can revise its guidance to explore different batch-
ing, evidence-selection, and reuse strategies within the same host
workflow.

evidence.excerpt:
On BrowseComp,OpenSaCimproves accuracy by 2.96 percent-
age points while reducing mean execution time by 30.3% (Table 2).
Across the 169 paired tasks,OpenSaCanswers 14 questions cor-
rectly that native retrieval misses, while native retrieval answers
nine thatOpenSaCmisses. Model token usage falls by 37.8%, ac-
companied by a 36.4% reduction in recorded model cost.
On WideSearch,OpenSaCreduces mean execution time by 29.5%,
saving about 227 seconds per task, while row F1 declines by 0.84
percentage points. Model token usage falls by 13.8% and recorded
model cost by 12.6%. The time reduction is similar across bench-
marks, but token and model-cost savings are larger on BrowseComp,
where accuracy also improves.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: The headline outcomes are measured on established external benchmarks (BrowseComp accuracy, WideSearch macro row F1) with audited decontamination and manual grading corrections, independent of the library and skill design.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: BrowseComp accuracy and WideSearch macro row F1, plus execution time, token counts, and recorded model cost, computed via the Harbor framework on paired task sets.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: The system under study is a fixed open-source library and companion skill with pre-specified guidance; no training, tuning, reward, or selection loop against the reported benchmarks is described.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Reported findings align accurately with the evaluation: OpenSaC demonstrated substantial latency and token reductions on both benchmarks, improved BrowseComp accuracy (+2.96%), and showed a minor drop in WideSearch row F1 (-0.84%).
primary.evaluation_assessment: The empirical evaluation on BrowseComp and WideSearch compares OpenSaC against native Codex web search across ~170 paired tasks per benchmark, reporting accuracy/F1, runtime, token counts, and cost under audited exclusions.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Evaluations were conducted on established external benchmarks with automated grading and audited data decontamination.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Standard benchmark test suites (BrowseComp accuracy and WideSearch macro row F1) run via the Harbor framework.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Pre-specified agent skill prompts and modular SDK runtime design without iterative model tuning or reward optimization.

primary.limitations: The authors transparently report the slight quality regression on WideSearch, benchmark task exclusions due to ground-truth leakage, and the need for future exploration into fine-tuning and adaptive skill optimization.
primary.method_assessment: The architecture cleanly decouples agent reasoning from programmatic execution, offering typed batch APIs, asynchronous dispatch, lifecycle management, and provider adapters.
primary.quality_rationale: The short paper delivers a well-defined systems contribution with practical relevance to deep research agents, accompanied by open-source code and clear, transparent empirical comparisons.
primary.scoped_contribution: OpenSaC is an open-source Python library and companion agent skill providing composable interfaces and runtime support for the Search-as-Code paradigm in coding agents.
